title: US Startup Reflect Orbital Wants to Sell Sunlight at Night — and India Is in Its Launch Plan
excerpt: The California firm plans some 50,000 mirror satellites to beam daylight after dark at a reported $5,000 an hour. Its first flights are booked with India's Skyroot Aerospace, and astronomers are furious.
body:
• California startup Reflect Orbital plans a constellation of around 50,000 satellites with mirrors to beam sunlight to Earth after dark — at a reported $5,000 an hour.
  • The FCC has approved its first demonstration satellite, Earendil-1, with an 18-by-18-metre mirror; the company has yet to launch anything.
  • India is built into the plan: Reflect has booked two dedicated rocket flights with Hyderabad-based Skyroot Aerospace.
  • Astronomers have attacked the plan as a threat to the night sky; the company says its ground test in California was fully permitted and that beams can avoid observatories.

The next subscription on offer could be sunlight itself. Reflect Orbital, a California startup, wants to deploy a constellation of around 50,000 satellites fitted with large mirrors that would reflect sunlight down to Earth after dark — "sunlight as a service," in its own framing — at a reported price of $5,000 for an hour of light, according to Fast Company.

How it would work

The satellites would orbit at roughly 625 kilometres, staying in sunlight while the ground below is in darkness, and angle their mirrors to cast a beam about 5 kilometres wide. Reflect says the light would be dimmable from "noon light to moonlight," and pitches uses from keeping solar farms generating after sunset to lighting disaster zones, search-and-rescue operations and work sites. With a reported price of $5,000 an hour — and reported annual contracts with minimum usage — critics assume the realistic customers are militaries and large industrial operators, whatever the altruistic branding. Sky & Telescope describes the $5,000 figure as the company's planned valuation of the service; no satellite has launched and no sale has been reported.

"One astrophysicist told Fast Company the 50,000-mirror plan is akin to "a bullet in your head," citing threats to the natural world and the future of astronomy."

Where the plan actually stands

Reflect has not launched a single satellite yet. In July, the FCC approved one demonstration satellite, Earendil-1, carrying an 18-by-18-metre mirror. On October 10, unable to test in orbit, the company simulated its beams with powerful spotlights near Lone Pine, California, inviting local volunteer search-and-rescue groups to practise night operations in the artificial light — a test that caught astronomers by surprise, Sky & Telescope reported. The company afterwards said the test was fully permitted and that it had notified Edwards Air Force Base and the local sheriff's department.

The India connection

India is not just a prospective customer; it is part of the launch plan. Reflect has booked two dedicated rocket flights with Skyroot Aerospace, the Hyderabad-based startup whose Vikram rockets launch from Indian soil — making India the launch state that would carry international responsibility for those satellites. Indian solar parks, among the largest in the world, are also the kind of customer the company's solar-after-dark pitch is aimed at.

The backlash

Astronomers have been blunt. One astrophysicist told Fast Company the 50,000-mirror plan is akin to "a bullet in your head," citing threats to the natural world and the future of astronomy. Princeton astrophysicist Gáspár Bakos told Sky & Telescope that "sunlight on demand" is "essentially ignoring all the progress we have made" on light pollution. Reflect responds that its beams can be aimed to avoid observatories and sensitive areas. Whether regulators — and the public — accept a night sky with an on-switch is a fight that will run long before the constellation does.
